papers.note: The standard taxonomy of bias sources and fairness definitions, which an audit needs before it can test anything.
papers.title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
papers.explain_beginner: This survey looks at how artificial intelligence can treat people unfairly. It gathers examples from real uses where such unfairness appeared. It sorts the reasons bias can enter AI systems. It also organizes the different ways researchers define fairness, so people can compare ideas. The paper reviews many areas of AI and describes unfair results researchers found and attempts to fix them. It says more work is needed. This matters because AI often helps make important choices, so unfair treatment can harm groups. The survey gives a shared starting point for spotting and discussing bias.
papers.explain_business: This survey explains that AI systems can make important decisions and may treat groups unfairly. It gathers real cases where bias appeared, identifies where bias can enter, and organizes the ways fairness is defined. It also reviews how different AI areas have shown unfair results and what researchers tried. For an executive, the practical message is that fairness needs attention during design and engineering. The paper provides a shared vocabulary and map of bias sources, which can guide how organizations discuss and review fairness. It also shows the field still lacks complete solutions, so more work is needed.
papers.explain_practitioner: This 2019 survey by Mehrabi and colleagues reviews bias and fairness in machine learning. It collects real applications where bias has appeared and lists where bias can come from. It builds a taxonomy of how fairness is defined proposed by machine learning researchers. It then examines several AI domains and subdomains, reporting unfair outcomes seen in leading methods and approaches used to address them. The main contribution is a structured map of bias sources and fairness concepts, plus a review of problems in specific domains and fixes. It notes that many open problems remain. For engineers, it offers a reference for framing audits and comparing fairness choices before testing.

papers.note: Organises mitigation into eleven method areas and lists open source libraries, which is practical for recommending remediation.
papers.title: Fairness in Machine Learning: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: This survey explains that machine learning can affect people in important ways, so companies and researchers must watch for unfair outcomes linked to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness literature is large and difficult for newcomers, so the authors map the main ideas and remedies. They group fixes by when they happen, before training, during training, and after training, then split these into eleven areas. They also cover fairness beyond simple yes or no predictions, including regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning, and point to publicly available software tools. It matters because it gives a practical starting point for reducing bias.
papers.explain_business: This survey says that when machine learning affects people, leaders need confidence that it will not create unexpected social harm, such as bias related to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness field is complex, so the authors provide a structured overview. They group remedies by when they are applied, before training, during training, and after training, with eleven method areas. They also cover settings beyond yes or no prediction and list publicly available software libraries. In practice, this helps executives decide how to assess and remediate fairness risks, where to look for tools, and why unresolved tensions require ongoing governance rather than a single fix.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey reviews fairness approaches for machine learning. It organizes mitigation methods by the stage at which they act, before training, during training, and after training. Within that structure, it identifies eleven method areas. The authors note that most published work focuses on yes or no prediction, but they also discuss fairness for regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning. They list publicly available software libraries. The key result is a practical map of the field, plus five unresolved tensions that summarize open fairness challenges. This helps researchers choose remediation strategies and locate tools, while seeing where evidence remains limited.

papers.note: Documents which groups have actually been harmed by educational algorithms, useful evidence for an education sector engagement.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias in Education
papers.journal: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
papers.explain_beginner: This review looks at bias in computer systems used in education. It gathers existing evidence about which groups have actually been harmed. The most studied groups are race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality. There is less evidence about students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families. The paper also examines where bias can enter when educational algorithms are built and used. It matters because schools increasingly rely on AI and other educational technology. If these tools treat some students unfairly, they can affect opportunities and outcomes. The authors call for a shift from not knowing where bias exists to identifying it, and from fairness toward equity. They note obstacles and suggest ways to reduce harm.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that educational AI and related technology can carry bias that harms particular student groups. The authors reviewed existing evidence and found that race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality are the best documented areas, while students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families are less understood. They also point to where bias can arise during development and deployment. In practice, leaders should not assume a tool is fair just because it is widely used. The paper supports decisions to demand evidence of unequal impacts, assess bias with appropriate metrics, address understudied groups, and invest in mitigation and equity efforts.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper is a review. It examines causes of bias in education, connects theoretical and formal fairness ideas to the steps used to build machine learning systems, and surveys metrics for measuring bias. Race or ethnicity, gender, and nationality have the most evidence. Students from poorer backgrounds, students with disabilities, and students from military families have less. The review identifies which stages and people in development and deployment are involved. Its contribution is a framework for moving from not knowing where bias exists to identifying it, and from fairness toward equity. It notes barriers and proposes four areas of work to reduce bias in AI and learning technology.

papers.note: Compares pre-, in- and post-processing mitigations and when each fits, which supports practical audit recommendations.
papers.title: A Review on Fairness in Machine Learning
papers.explain_beginner: Machine learning now helps make many important decisions, such as who gets a loan, a job, or a place at college. This review explains that these systems can be unfair even when nobody intends harm. It gathers common ways to define fairness, ways to measure it, and methods to improve it. Those methods are grouped by when they act, before training, during training, or after training. The authors compare them to see which approach suits different situations. This matters because people need to know how to check and improve automated decisions that affect their lives.
papers.explain_business: Organizations increasingly use machine learning for decisions in hiring, lending, education, healthcare, and other areas. This review shows that unfair outcomes can occur even without deliberate bias. It explains how to identify and measure fairness and compares methods for improving it before, during, or after model development. The authors assess which methods fit different situations. For executives, this means fairness should be treated as a managed part of AI projects, not an afterthought. The paper can inform decisions about when to audit models, which mitigation stage to choose, and how to set practical fairness checks before deploying automated systems.
papers.explain_practitioner: This paper is a review of fairness in machine learning, focused mainly on classification. It covers why bias and unfairness arise in algorithms, along with how fairness is commonly defined and measured. The authors organize methods that improve fairness into three stages, before model training, during model training, and after model training. They then compare these approaches to clarify which ones fit different scenarios. The review also looks at newer research areas in fairness outside classification. For engineers and researchers, the value is a structured map of available techniques and when each may be suitable, which can guide method selection and fairness audits in practical machine learning work.

papers.note: The canonical bias survey, with three taxonomies covering metrics, datasets and mitigation stages.
papers.title: Bias and Fairness in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: The question here is simple to state and hard to answer. When a language model writes text, does it treat different groups of people, genders, races, religions, unfairly, and if so how would anyone even measure that. This survey does not run new experiments on a model. Instead it reads through the large and scattered body of prior research on bias in large language models and organizes it into one coherent picture. The authors sort out the many different ways researchers have tried to detect unfair treatment, looking at word associations inside the model, at probabilities it assigns to different groups, at the actual sentences it generates, and the many different fixes that have been tried, changing training data, changing the training process, adjusting the model afterward, filtering its output. What it found is less a single answer than a map, bias shows up in many forms depending on how you look for it, and no single metric or fix covers all of them. What it does not settle is which definition of fairness is correct, since different papers use incompatible definitions, and it cannot say which specific mitigation works best in a live product, only how the field's own techniques compare to each other on paper.
papers.explain_business: Nothing here is a plug in fix a company can buy today. What changes for a buyer or deployer of language model products is the vocabulary and the checklist. Before this kind of survey, teams often picked one fairness test almost at random and declared a model checked. The taxonomy makes clear that a model can pass a word embedding bias test and still produce biased text in generation, because these operate at different levels and do not agree with each other. Practically, a procurement or safety review should ask which stage of the pipeline a vendor's bias testing covers, pre training data audits, in training adjustments, or output filtering, since passing one stage says nothing about the others. The compliance relevant fact is that no evaluation in this survey is a certification, each is a diagnostic tool that surfaces certain failure modes and misses others. Right now this is mainly a research and due diligence resource. It becomes operationally important the moment a regulator or internal policy requires documented bias testing, at which point this taxonomy is a reasonable checklist for what a real testing program should cover across the whole model lifecycle.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper is a structured literature synthesis, not new experiments, built around three taxonomies. Bias evaluation metrics are grouped by the level at which they operate, embedding based, probability based, comparing likelihoods assigned to different demographic terms, or generated text based, scoring actual outputs for stereotypes or toxicity. Evaluation datasets are grouped by structure, counterfactual pairs that swap a demographic term, or prompts meant to elicit biased continuations, each tagged by which harm and social group it targets. Mitigation techniques are classified by when they intervene, pre processing the training data, in training changes to the objective, intra processing changes to decoding at inference time, or post processing edits to the finished output. The paper also releases a consolidated list of public bias evaluation datasets, useful because they were previously scattered across dozens of individual papers. The authors state plainly that open problems remain, including that many metrics measure different underlying constructs so results do not transfer cleanly between them, a limitation that matters if a team picks one fairness metric and assumes it covers the others.

papers.note: Traces where bias enters a clinical workflow, from acquisition to labelling, which tells an audit where to sample evidence.
papers.title: Algorithm fairness in artificial intelligence for medicine and healthcare

papers.note: Early work defining representational bias sources and pushing the performance fairness frontier rather than trading one off.
papers.title: Towards Understanding and Mitigating Social Biases in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at a specific kind of unfairness called representational bias, which is when a model's stereotypes about a group show up in the words it generates, for example consistently pairing certain jobs or traits with one gender or race even when nothing in the prompt calls for it. Researchers cared about this because language models were starting to get used in healthcare, legal, and social science settings, where a subtle stereotype baked into generated text could quietly influence a real decision. The paper's contribution is defining several distinct sources of this kind of bias more precisely than earlier work, then building new benchmarks and metrics to measure them, and finally testing a method to reduce the bias during text generation itself. It found that its method could reduce measured stereotyping while keeping the generated text just as useful, an outcome the authors describe as improving the tradeoff between fairness and performance rather than trading one for the other. It does not claim to eliminate representational bias, and it does not establish that its new benchmarks capture every way stereotyping can appear in generated text.
papers.explain_business: The operational fact for anyone deploying a language model in a regulated or high stakes setting, healthcare intake, legal drafting, HR screening text, is that debiasing is not automatically a quality tax. This paper's central selling point is evidence that a well designed intervention can cut measured stereotyping without a proportional loss in output quality, which answers a common objection from product teams that fairness work necessarily degrades the product. The practical caveat is that the benchmarks used to show this were built by the same team for this specific study, so a business adopting a similar method should still validate it against its own use case and its own definition of unacceptable stereotyping, rather than assuming the reported numbers transfer directly. This is largely still a research technique rather than an off the shelf enterprise tool. It becomes relevant to a deployment decision once a vendor claims its bias mitigation happens at generation time, since that is the specific mechanism this line of research popularized, and a buyer can reasonably ask what benchmark was used to validate that claim.
papers.explain_practitioner: The method operates at generation time rather than requiring a full retrain, intervening in how text is produced so that stereotyped associations are suppressed while the model keeps most of its original language ability. To evaluate this the authors built new benchmarks and metrics specifically for representational bias, judging existing bias benchmarks too narrow for the sources of bias they had just defined. The key result is a demonstrated improvement in what the paper calls the performance fairness Pareto frontier, meaning at a given level of text quality the method achieves less measured bias than prior baselines, or at a given level of bias reduction it preserves more text quality, rather than only reporting a bias score in isolation. This framing matters because many earlier debiasing methods reduced bias only by degrading fluency or task accuracy. The paper's own scope limitation is that it focuses on the specific representational biases it defines around stereotyping, and it does not fully resolve how well the approach generalizes to bias types and languages outside what its new benchmarks were built to measure.

papers.note: Addresses the common case where the client holds no protected attribute data, which otherwise blocks a fairness test entirely.
papers.title: Fairer machine learning in the real world: Mitigating discrimination without collecting sensitive data

papers.note: The most referenced open bias audit toolkit, which gives an audit a reproducible way to compute group metrics.
papers.title: Aequitas: A Bias and Fairness Audit Toolkit
papers.explain_beginner: This paper introduces Aequitas, a free tool that helps check whether artificial intelligence systems treat different groups of people fairly. It can look at groups based on things like race, gender, or religion. The authors note that many ways to measure fairness exist, but people often do not agree on which one to use, and few practical tools are available. Aequitas lets users test a model against several fairness measures for different groups. This matters because AI is used in decisions that affect people, and without regular checks, it may unintentionally harm some groups. The tool aims to make fairness checks easier and more common.
papers.explain_business: This paper describes Aequitas, a free open source tool for checking whether an AI system treats different groups fairly. It lets teams test models against multiple fairness measures for groups such as race, gender, or religion. The authors say that although many fairness measures exist, organizations often lack a standard way to apply them. Aequitas is designed to fit into normal machine learning work. In practice, it gives leaders a way to add fairness checks before deploying AI that makes decisions about people. That can inform decisions about whether and how to deploy a model, and it supports more equitable choices.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors present Aequitas, an open source toolkit for auditing machine learning models for bias and fairness. It plugs into an existing machine learning workflow and lets users compute several fairness metrics across multiple population subgroups. The work addresses a practical gap: many fairness definitions and bias metrics exist, but there is little agreement on which to choose and few resources to apply them. Aequitas makes these checks easier and repeatable. Its key contribution is operationalizing group fairness testing so data scientists, researchers, and policymakers can compare model behavior across subgroups and make more informed decisions about deploying algorithmic systems.

papers.note: Explains proxy discrimination persisting after sensitive attributes are removed, which is the point clients most often get wrong.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias: From Discrimination Discovery to Fairness-aware Data Mining
papers.journal: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining

papers.note: Finds different fairness metrics disagreeing on the same case, which is why an audit must state which metric it used and why.
papers.title: Bias and Unfairness in Machine Learning Models: A Systematic Review on Datasets, Tools, Fairness Metrics, and Identification and Mitigation Methods
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at research on fairness in machine learning, the systems that make decisions from data. The authors searched several databases and selected 45 studies from 2017 to 2022. They found that most work tries to find or reduce bias, using datasets, tools, and fairness measures. Common measures include Equalized Odds, Opportunity Equality, and Demographic Parity. The studies cover areas like criminal justice, finance, education, pricing, and health. A key point is that different fairness measures can disagree about the same case. So an audit should say which measure it used and why. More varied research is still needed.
papers.explain_business: This review shows that fairness in machine learning is not a single, settled standard. Organizations using automated decisions should expect different fairness measures to give conflicting answers for the same case. That means an audit or governance process must name the fairness measure used and explain why it fits the context. The paper also finds limited research on multiclass and multimetric settings, so many methods remain binary focused. For executives, this supports cautious deployment, clear documentation, and asking vendors or teams which fairness definition they applied. It also informs investment in broader testing across model types and use cases before relying on fairness claims.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a PRISMA systematic review, registered on OSF, searching Scopus, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from 2021 to early 2022. They identified 128 articles from 2017 to 2022 and selected 45 after refining the search and applying screening rules. The review maps datasets, tools, metrics, and methods for finding and reducing bias. It reports bias from data, algorithms, and user interaction linked to preprocessing, during processing, and postprocessing fixes. Equalized Odds, Opportunity Equality, and Demographic Parity are primary metrics. Aequitas is most cited, though many tools lack empirical use. Result: fairness metrics can disagree for one use case, and multiclass or multimetric studies are scarce.

papers.note: Argues technical neutrality can increase harm, which an audit should raise when a client claims bias is solved by dropping a variable.
papers.title: Ethical limitations of algorithmic fairness solutions in health care machine learning.
papers.explain_beginner: The paper warns that bias in health data is an ethical problem for medical artificial intelligence. Fairness methods try to make models neutral. They might remove race or gender, force groups to have similar error rates, make predictions independent of identity after accounting for risk, or balance benefits and harms. The authors argue that focusing on technical neutrality can make harm worse. Removing a variable is often ineffective and can make unfair treatment worse. So when a client says bias is solved by dropping a variable, an audit should challenge that. This matters because fairness in health care is not only technical.
papers.explain_business: The paper says bias in health data is an ethical threat to medical AI. Fairness methods may make models appear neutral by removing race or gender, matching error rates between groups, making outcomes independent of identity, or balancing benefits and harms. But the authors argue that a technical fix can worsen harm. Dropping a variable is often ineffective and can make unfair treatment worse. For executives, a client claim that bias is solved by deleting a variable should trigger scrutiny. Decisions about using health AI should include ethical review and audits, not just mathematical fairness checks. It informs whether to accept a fairness fix as sufficient.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper examines fairness approaches meant to make health care machine learning models neutral. These methods limit bias in predictions for groups defined by race or gender. They may drop those variables, require similar error rates across groups, make outcomes independent of identity after adjusting for risk, or mathematically balance benefits and harms. The authors argue that making a model neutral in a technical way can worsen harm instead of solving ethical problems. They note that leaving out a variable is widely seen as ineffective and can make unfair treatment worse. The key practical point is that audits should question claims that bias is solved simply by removing a variable.

papers.note: Classifies metrics as bias preserving or bias transforming against EU law, which turns a technical choice into a legal exposure an audit can flag.
papers.title: Bias Preservation in Machine Learning: The Legality of Fairness Metrics Under EU Non-Discrimination Law

papers.note: Sets out twelve components of a psychological audit, which is one of the few published specifications of what an AI audit should contain.
papers.title: Auditing the AI auditors: A framework for evaluating fairness and bias in high stakes AI predictive models.

papers.note: Summarises bias types, metrics and tooling for clinical models, a convenient single reference for a healthcare engagement.
papers.title: Algorithmic fairness in computational medicine
papers.explain_beginner: This paper is a review, not a new experiment. It explains that machine learning is used more often to help doctors make choices. Such software can treat people in different groups unfairly, for example some ethnic minorities, and that can harm their health and daily life. The authors gather what is known about this problem in medicine. They describe kinds of bias, ways to measure fairness, methods to reduce bias, and common software tools for checking and fixing it. It matters because it gives one starting point for people who want to build or use clinical AI more fairly.
papers.explain_business: For an executive, this paper is a single reference for a healthcare engagement. It explains that clinical machine learning can create unfair outcomes for patient subgroups, including some ethnic minority patients, with possible harm to health and daily life. It gathers bias types, fairness metrics, mitigation methods, and software tools for evaluation and reduction. In practice, it can inform decisions about how to evaluate and address fairness in clinical AI projects. It does not offer a new product or trial result.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors produced a broad review of fairness for computational medicine. They organize the field by covering several bias types that can affect clinical machine learning, the measures used to quantify fairness, and approaches intended to reduce bias. They also survey widely used software packages and utilities for checking and lowering bias. The key result is a consolidated reference that connects these ideas for researchers and people applying them. It does not report a new model or clinical trial. Instead, it offers a structured overview to support fairer development and assessment of clinical decision making systems.

papers.note: Separates intrinsic from extrinsic bias and organises evaluation by data, model and output level.
papers.title: Bias in Large Language Models: Origin, Evaluation, and Mitigation
papers.explain_beginner: This paper asks where bias in large language models actually comes from, not just whether it exists. Most people know that chatbots can produce stereotyped or unfair text, but this survey tries to trace that back to its source. It splits the causes into two kinds, bias built into the model itself from how it was trained, called intrinsic bias, and bias that only shows up once the model is used for a specific task, called extrinsic bias. Intrinsic bias comes from things like which groups are over or under represented in the training text, from data scraped mostly from English speaking, Western sources, and from ambiguous language where gender neutral words get silently associated with one gender. Extrinsic bias shows up later, for example in how a model resolves pronouns or judges sentiment differently depending on the names or groups mentioned in a task. The paper finds that these two sources need different tests and different fixes. It does not resolve the field's biggest open question, whether bias can be fully removed rather than just measured and reduced, and the authors say directly that the problem stays complex and ongoing as models keep changing.
papers.explain_business: For a team choosing how to test or fix bias in a deployed model, this paper is useful mainly as an inventory rather than a specific recommendation. It shows that data level fixes, curating or rebalancing training data, and post model fixes, filtering or adjusting output after generation, are different levers, so a vendor who says they mitigated bias needs to specify at which stage, since a post processing filter does nothing to repair biased internal representations and vice versa. The practical risk this surfaces is the accuracy fairness tradeoff the authors flag, meaning a business that pushes hard on one fairness metric without checking task accuracy could ship a model that is measurably fairer on paper but worse at the actual job. There is no finished product or standard here, this is a map of research directions as of late 2024, not a compliance framework. It becomes operationally relevant once a company needs to justify to auditors, customers, or regulators which of these four evaluation levels and three mitigation stages its own testing actually covers, since most vendor bias claims today only test one of the four.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper organizes evaluation into four levels, data level checks looking at representation, imbalance, and source skew in the training corpus, model level checks using fairness metrics like equal opportunity and predictive parity plus interpretability tools such as SHAP and LIME, output level checks comparing outputs across counterfactual inputs and scoring stereotype and toxicity content, and a fourth human involved level using expert review. On mitigation it lays out three stages, pre model methods like counterfactual data augmentation and resampling, intra model methods like dropout regularization and causal inference during training, and post model methods applied after training such as Self Debias, SENT DEBIAS, INLP, and causal prompting. Rather than proposing one new method, it maps which techniques exist at each stage and what they target. The authors' own stated limitation matters here, they note that biases are context dependent and shift over time, that model scale makes comprehensive identification harder, and that fixing bias often trades off against accuracy, so a technique that reduces one measured bias can quietly hurt task performance elsewhere.

papers.note: Splits fairness work by model scale and training paradigm, which matters when advising on fine tuning versus prompting.
papers.title: A Survey on Fairness in Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models learn from huge amounts of text written by people, and that text carries the biases and stereotypes present in society. This means the models can end up treating groups of people unfairly, for example by favoring certain genders or ethnicities in the responses they produce. This paper is a broad survey that pulls together the research on making these language models fairer. The authors point out that fixing bias looks different depending on the size and type of the model. For smaller, more customizable models, researchers can dig into the model's internal workings and retrain or adjust it directly. For today's largest models, which are mostly used through prompts rather than retrained from scratch, fixing bias mostly means clever prompt design or lightweight fine tuning after the fact. The survey catalogs many ways to measure bias and many ways to reduce it, but it also concludes that no single fix works reliably across every situation, and that current tools for detecting and measuring bias in the largest models are still immature and inconsistent with each other.
papers.explain_business: For a business buying or deploying a large language model, this survey is a reminder that bias reduction is not a solved, one time fix, and no available metric fully certifies a model as fair. Vendors may report favorable scores on one fairness benchmark while the model still behaves unevenly across other measures or real use cases, because different fairness tests often do not agree with one another. Practically, companies should test any deployed model against their own use cases and demographic groups rather than trusting a single published benchmark score, and should expect that prompt based mitigations, such as adding fairness instructions to prompts, are the main lightweight tool for today's largest commercial models, though the paper notes such fixes are not always stable. There is a real cost implication too, since current best practice debiasing, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, is expensive and resource intensive, so budgeting for ongoing fairness auditing, not a single upfront check, is the more realistic approach for any organization deploying these models at scale.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a survey rather than an original experiment, organizing prior work on fairness in large language models around a size based taxonomy: medium sized models, addressed through pre-training and fine-tuning, and today's largest models, addressed mainly through prompting since their internal representations are less accessible. For medium sized models it catalogs intrinsic bias metrics such as SEAT, CrowS-Pairs, and WinoBias, and extrinsic bias benchmarks such as BOLD and BBQ, alongside debiasing methods spanning pre-processing counterfactual data augmentation, in-processing disentanglement and contrastive learning, and post-processing embedding correction. For large models it reviews newer benchmarks like BiasAsker and FairPrism, and covers RLHF instruction tuning and prompt engineering as the dominant mitigations. The finding that matters most is the observation that intrinsic and extrinsic bias measures are not reliably correlated, so fairer internal representations do not guarantee fairer outputs, and different fairness metrics often disagree. A limitation the authors name directly is that benchmarks for large scale models remain neither diverse nor comprehensive enough, and low cost, reliable debiasing methods for large models are still lacking compared to resource heavy RLHF pipelines.

papers.note: Applies fairness metrics to real mortgage data and notes the explainability cost of better models, a trade-off lenders must document.
papers.title: Algorithmic Fairness

papers.note: Summarises evaluation metrics plus the toolkits and datasets available to run them, a practical starting kit.
papers.title: Fairness in Large Language Models: A Taxonomic Survey
papers.explain_beginner: This survey asks a basic question, once a language model is expected to be fair, what does fairness even mean for a system like this, and how is that different from fairness in older, simpler machine learning models. The authors point out that fairness research built for things like loan approval algorithms does not transfer cleanly to a model that generates open ended text, because there is no single protected outcome to check, like approve or deny, there is an entire generated sentence that can be subtly biased in tone, association, or omission. The paper works through why large language models pick up bias in the first place, tracing it to training data and design choices, then surveys how researchers try to measure fairness and the tools built to promote it. It found that the field has produced many metrics and toolkits but no unified standard, and that fairness concepts genuinely need new definitions for generative systems rather than borrowed ones. It does not settle which definition should become the standard, and it explicitly leaves that question open for future work rather than answering it.
papers.explain_business: The direct business relevance is as a reference document when scoping a fairness audit for a language model product, not as a ready made compliance tool. Because the paper catalogs existing toolkits and datasets for bias evaluation, a team building an internal review process can use it to avoid reinventing evaluation infrastructure that already exists in the open research community. The risk it implicitly flags is that fairness metrics built for older classification systems, the kind many compliance teams already know, do not directly apply to generative text systems, so a company relying on legacy fairness testing frameworks may be checking the wrong thing entirely for a chatbot or writing assistant. There is no dollar figure or deployment timeline attached to this paper, it is foundational rather than applied. It becomes operationally useful the moment an organization needs to build or select a bias testing toolkit for a language model product, since the survey's compiled resource list shortens that search, though someone still has to validate that a chosen toolkit actually works for the specific language and use case being deployed.
papers.explain_practitioner: Published in ACM SIGKDD Explorations Newsletter, this is a categorical survey rather than an experimental paper. It begins with the factors that introduce bias into large language models, moves through how fairness is conceptualized specifically for these systems as distinct from classical machine learning fairness, and then summarizes both the metrics used to evaluate bias and the algorithms proposed to promote fairness. It also compiles toolkits and datasets built for bias evaluation, functioning as a resource index for anyone building an evaluation pipeline. A related tutorial version of this work, presented at a major data mining conference as a three hour session, signals that the field treated this taxonomy as a teaching reference rather than a one off publication. The authors close by naming open research challenges and unanswered questions directly, without resolving them, which is the honest limitation of any survey of this kind, it maps the literature accurately but cannot tell a practitioner which specific metric or toolkit will generalize to a new model or a new language, since most of the underlying studies were built and tested on English language models.

papers.note: 22 of 24 studies found bias, with gender bias in 15 of 16, the clearest prevalence evidence for medical deployments.
papers.title: Evaluating and addressing demographic disparities in medical large language models: a systematic review
papers.journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
papers.explain_beginner: The question behind this review is whether the AI chatbots increasingly tested for medical use actually treat different kinds of patients the same way, for instance whether a model's suggested diagnosis or treatment plan changes just because a patient is described as a different gender or race with everything else about the case held constant. This matters because these systems are being piloted for tasks like triage, patient education, and clinical decision support, and unequal treatment baked into the model could quietly widen existing health disparities rather than close them. Rather than testing a model itself, this is a systematic review that gathered and graded 24 existing studies published between 2018 and mid 2024 that had already tested medical large language models for this kind of demographic disparity. It found that the overwhelming majority of those studies, 22 out of 24, detected some form of bias, most commonly related to gender and to race or ethnicity. It does not establish how large these effects are in an actual clinical setting, since the underlying studies were mostly test bench evaluations, not real patient outcomes, and the review's own authors note that studies finding no bias are less likely to get published in the first place.
papers.explain_business: For a hospital system or health technology buyer evaluating a medical large language model, the concrete fact from this review is that demographic bias testing found a problem in the near totality of prior evaluations, 22 of 24 studies, so the reasonable default assumption should be that an untested model likely carries some demographic disparity until proven otherwise for that specific model and use case. The operational risk is concentrated in gender and race or ethnicity, the two categories flagged most often, which maps directly onto categories many healthcare equity and anti-discrimination policies already require organizations to monitor. The review's finding that prompt engineering mitigation was inconsistent means a vendor claiming to have resolved bias through prompting alone should be asked for study specific evidence, not just a general assurance. This becomes compliance relevant right now for any organization piloting generative AI in clinical decision support, patient communication, or triage, since demographic disparity testing before deployment is the direct, actionable step this review's own findings point to, even though the review stops short of certifying any single mitigation method as reliable.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a systematic review, not an original experiment, screened across five databases and appraised for quality using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, covering 24 eligible studies from January 2018 through July 2024. The headline numbers are specific, bias was detected in 22 of 24 studies overall, gender bias appeared in 15 of 16 studies that tested for it, and racial or ethnic bias appeared in 10 of 11 studies that tested for it, with only two studies reporting minimal or no bias in their particular context. Where studies tested fixes, the review found mitigation attempts relied mostly on prompt engineering, adjusting the wording given to the model, and reported inconsistent effectiveness rather than a reliable fix. The review does not benchmark one large language model against another head to head, it aggregates findings across many different models and study designs, which is itself a limitation the authors acknowledge. Their stated caveats include real publication bias risk, since null results are published less often, and a gap toward intersectional analysis and non-Western populations, meaning most existing evidence reflects a narrower slice of demographic and cultural contexts than the technology is being deployed into.

papers.note: A human-in-the-loop debiasing tool that records the reasoning behind each change, which produces the audit trail fairness work usually lacks.
papers.title: D-BIAS: A Causality-Based Human-in-the-Loop System for Tackling Algorithmic Bias
papers.journal: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

papers.note: Argues outcome auditing is legally permitted and necessary because bias often sits outside the code, which supports the case for external review.
papers.title: Auditing Algorithms for Discrimination
papers.journal: University of Pennsylvania Law Review Online
papers.explain_beginner: Kim's paper argues that fair code is not enough to stop discrimination. Bias can enter through social conditions and structural inequality, not only through programming choices. Methods such as randomization or fixed rules cannot promise unbiased results. Even carefully built systems may carry forward old prejudices. So the paper says we must watch how systems actually behave and study their outcomes. This kind of auditing is necessary to find and correct unfair outcomes. It is also allowed by law, according to Kim. The point matters because unfair outcomes can go unnoticed without outcome review.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper means that fairness cannot be guaranteed by good design or technical safeguards alone. Automated decisions may still produce biased results because bias can come from broader social conditions. The practical step is to audit actual outcomes after deployment and use external review where needed. Kim argues this is legally permitted, so companies can act voluntarily to find and correct bias. A key legal point is that algorithms may be revised prospectively to remove discrimination. The decision this informs is to fund ongoing outcome monitoring and correction, rather than treating fairness as a single engineering task.
papers.explain_practitioner: Kim's essay replies to Kroll and colleagues, who favored technical fairness methods over transparency. Kim argues that for discrimination, such methods cannot stand alone. Bias often arises from social processes outside the software, so randomization or preset decision constraints cannot ensure unbiased results. Carefully built systems can still reproduce existing prejudice or structural disadvantage. The practical response is to inspect real outcomes, not just design, because only observed effects reveal discrimination. Kim examines law and concludes that auditing is permitted. The contrary reading, Kim says, misinterprets Ricci v. DeStefano. That ruling was narrow, about adverse action against identifiable people by race, while prospective algorithm changes to remove bias remain lawful.

papers.note: Uses the COMPAS case to show scale turning individual errors into systematic discrimination, which is the argument for auditing before scaling.
papers.title: Algorithmic Fairness in AI
papers.explain_beginner: A 2016 investigation looked at COMPAS, a machine learning tool used in the U.S. legal system to give defendants scores about how likely they are to offend again after release. It found the tool was more likely to wrongly label Black defendants as high risk and less likely to wrongly label them low risk than white defendants. These mistakes can affect bail, probation, and early release, so they matter greatly. The paper argues that when such tools are used widely, small individual errors can become widespread unfairness, so fairness should be checked before scaling.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper warns that AI tools can create unfair outcomes at scale, not just isolated mistakes. The COMPAS example shows a tool that wrongly marked Black defendants as high risk more often than white defendants, with serious effects on bail, probation, and release. Because these tools learn from past data and then decide many cases, biased patterns can become widespread and expose organizations to equal opportunity violations. The practical decision is to check AI systems for fairness before broad use, especially in areas like recruiting, credit, pricing, and personalized advertising.
papers.explain_practitioner: This discussion paper examines fairness in AI through the COMPAS case. COMPAS is a tool that learns from data to predict repeat offenses in the U.S. legal system. It gives defendants scores meant to show how likely they are to offend again after release. ProPublica's analysis found higher rates of wrongly marking Black defendants as high risk and lower rates of wrongly marking them low risk than for white defendants. The paper explains that such tools learn from past data that may be biased, and once trained, they can decide many future cases, turning individual errors into widespread unfairness. It calls for fairness checks before scaling.

papers.note: Finds performance on commonsense tasks varies by culture and by the language the question is asked in, which is a concrete measurement of a bias usually discussed abstractly.
papers.title: Understanding the Capabilities and Limitations of Large Language Models for Cultural Commonsense
papers.explain_beginner: Common sense, the everyday background knowledge people use without thinking, is not actually the same everywhere. What counts as normal food, clothing, or etiquette varies by culture, so this paper asked whether AI language models understand common sense consistently across different countries or whether they secretly know some cultures better than others. The researchers tested several well known models, including GPT-4, on culture specific knowledge questions about five countries, the United States, China, India, Iran, and Kenya, asked in five different languages. They found real and sometimes large gaps, GPT-4 was noticeably less accurate on questions about Iran than about the United States or China, and results got substantially worse when questions were asked in Hindi rather than English. The paper also found that when a model was asked to name a country matching some described custom, it named the United States far more often than other countries, suggesting the training data itself skews toward some cultures more than others.
papers.explain_business: Companies deploying LLM based products internationally, for customer service, content moderation, or localization, should treat this paper's finding of real, measured accuracy gaps by culture and by query language as evidence, not speculation, that a single model tuned and tested in English will perform unevenly across global markets. The roughly 15 percentage point accuracy gap between US related and Iran related cultural questions for even the strongest model tested, GPT-4, and the additional drop when prompting in a non-English language such as Hindi, means launching the same model configuration into every market without local testing risks a measurably worse user experience in underrepresented regions. This applies now to any customer facing deployment spanning multiple countries or languages, and the practical response the paper supports is market specific evaluation before launch rather than assuming benchmark scores measured in English transfer evenly worldwide.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors evaluated GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, and several open models including LLaMA2, Vicuna, and Falcon on cultural commonsense using three existing resources, GeoMLAMA's culture specific assertions, CANDLE's cultural knowledge spanning food and rituals, and GenericsKB-Best for general assertion verification, across five countries and five languages. GPT-4 scored highest overall but still showed a real accuracy gap by culture, around 0.81 on US related questions and 0.85 on China related questions versus roughly 0.70 on Iran related questions, and multilingual prompting in Hindi produced the weakest results across models. Open models like LLaMA2 showed far larger, sometimes drastic, performance swings when cultural context was added compared to GPT-4's relative stability. A separate country association test found the US named roughly 6.8 times more often than Kenya as the source of a general commonsense statement. The authors explicitly note their evaluation datasets are English only in construction even when translated, and that country is an imperfect proxy for culture since factors like religion and regional wealth were not tested separately.

papers.note: Digital ageism is rarely covered elsewhere, and this mitigates it without touching model parameters.
papers.title: Mitigating Age-Related Bias in Large Language Models: Strategies for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Development
papers.explain_beginner: Most bias research on language models focuses on gender or race, and this paper instead asks whether these systems treat older and younger people unfairly, a problem it calls digital ageism, and if so whether that unfair treatment can be fixed without retraining the model from scratch. The authors built a system that lets a language model check its own answers for age bias and revise them, either alone or by having multiple model instances debate and reach consensus on a fairer answer, using a training method called reinforcement learning to guide the correction and a human in the loop to supervise it. A second idea in the paper has the model deliberately imagine the question from the perspective of a different age group before answering, to catch bias that a straight answer would miss. Tested across several datasets, the resulting system, which the authors call FairLLM, reduced measured age bias more than the comparison methods they tested. What the paper does not settle is whether this generalizes to age related situations outside the specific evaluation datasets used, and it does not change the underlying model's parameters, so the bias is corrected downstream each time rather than removed from the model's core knowledge.
papers.explain_business: The specific capability this introduces is a way to reduce age bias in an already deployed language model without the cost of retraining it, which matters for any company using language models in contexts covered by age discrimination law, hiring text generation, insurance or lending communications, eldercare or youth focused products, and customer service scripts. Because FairLLM works as a wrapper around inference rather than a retraining pipeline, it is cheaper to trial than a full model fine tune, but it adds a real operating cost, since the debate based cooperative mode runs multiple model calls per response, meaning higher API or compute spend for every fairer answer produced. This is a research prototype published with its code released on a public academic software repository, not a commercial product, so a business would need engineering effort to adapt it. It is relevant now for any organization already worried about age discrimination exposure in AI generated customer facing text, and becomes more broadly relevant once age bias testing becomes a named requirement in AI governance frameworks the way gender and race testing already is in several jurisdictions.
papers.explain_practitioner: The method is a two stage, inference time bias mitigation framework called FairLLM, meaning it works without retraining or fine tuning the underlying model. It offers two operating modes, self bias mitigation, where a single model assesses and revises its own output for age bias autonomously, and cooperative bias mitigation, where multiple language model instances debate a response and converge on a less biased answer through consensus. Both are layered with reinforcement learning and a human in the loop mechanism, and the paper adds an empathetic perspective exchange step that reframes the context given to the model before it answers, aimed at producing responses more appropriate across different age groups. Evaluated across multiple datasets, FairLLM outperformed the existing bias mitigation techniques the authors compared it against on fairness metrics. Because it is a training free, decoding time intervention, its main tradeoff is added inference cost and latency from running extra self assessment or multi model debate steps for every response, a real constraint any adopter would need to measure directly for their own workload, since the published evaluation focuses on fairness metrics rather than latency or serving cost.

papers.note: Considers how people change behaviour in response to a model, which means fairness at the prediction alone is not enough.
papers.title: Strategic Best-Response Fairness Framework for Fair Machine Learning
papers.explain_beginner: Machine learning systems often make decisions about people, like who gets a loan or a job. Usually, fairness is checked only by looking at the predictions themselves. This paper says that is not enough, because people change their behavior based on those predictions. For example, if a system seems biased, people might give up trying. The authors introduce a new idea called strategic best-response fairness. It asks whether two groups that start out the same end up putting in the same effort and getting the same results. They found that many common fairness methods do not achieve this, but one method, equalized odds, does, though it has practical problems. The paper argues that fairness must consider how people react, not just the prediction.
papers.explain_business: This research shows that fair predictions alone may not prevent discrimination. People change their behavior based on how algorithms treat them, so a model that looks fair can still lead to unequal effort and outcomes. The paper introduces strategic best-response fairness, which checks whether groups that start out identical end up with the same behavior and results. It finds that common fairness methods like demographic parity do not guarantee this, while equalized odds does but with practical drawbacks. For executives, this means fairness audits should include behavioral responses, not just prediction metrics. Decisions about deploying ML should consider whether the system encourages equal effort and outcomes across groups, and may require designing algorithms specifically for this goal.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper proposes strategic best-response fairness (SBR-fairness) as a framework for fair machine learning. It moves beyond fairness in prediction alone, arguing that individuals may alter their behavior in response to algorithmic decisions. The key question is whether an algorithm trained on potentially biased data leads to identical equilibrium behaviors across subpopulations that are ex ante identical. The authors evaluate common fair-ML algorithms. They find that color-blindness and demographic parity criteria do not always achieve SBR fairness, meaning disparities in effort and outcomes can persist. Equalized odds does achieve SBR fairness, but it has several practical limitations. The work suggests SBR fairness is a necessary condition for breaking discrimination cycles and offers a complementary assessment tool.

papers.note: Prices fairness breaches against the AI Act fine tiers using 12.4 million real underwriting records, a rare quantified case.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias Under the EU AI Act: Compliance Risk, Capital Strain, and Pricing Distortions in Life and Health Insurance Underwriting
papers.explain_beginner: Insurance companies increasingly use computer models to decide how much people pay for life and health coverage. This paper asks whether those pricing models are unfair to certain groups, and if so, what it would cost insurers to fix that unfairness under Europe's new AI Act. Using millions of real insurance records from four European insurers, the researchers found that people in the lowest income group were charged noticeably more than a fair calculation would justify, about 5.8 percent more for life insurance and 7.2 percent more for health insurance, which breaches an informal regulatory tolerance level. Digging into why, they found the overcharging usually was not caused directly by protected traits like income itself, but by indirect stand-ins for them, such as certain job categories or living in a poorer neighborhood. The good news is that available bias-correction techniques closed most of this unfair gap, while adding only a modest amount to the extra capital insurers must hold to stay financially safe under EU solvency rules.
papers.explain_business: For insurers, and for regulators or investors watching them, this study puts a number on something usually discussed only in the abstract, unfair AI-driven pricing carries a measurable capital cost, not just a reputational or legal one. The paper estimates roughly 22 basis points of extra required capital tied to biased pricing outcomes, but shows that applying a bias-correction technique called adversarial debiasing removes most of the unfairness while adding a comparatively small amount, about 14 basis points, to that capital requirement, at an estimated cost near 4.8 million euros for a mid-sized carrier. That makes proactive fairness testing look like a reasonable investment compared with the alternative, since the authors also calculate that fines become more expensive than fixing the problem once the chance of getting caught passes about 8.9 percent. The catch is that the underlying unfairness often comes from indirect variables, like job category or neighborhood, rather than obviously protected attributes, so insurers cannot assume removing protected fields from their models is enough to comply.
papers.explain_practitioner: Using 12.4 million quote-bind-claim records from four pan-European insurers spanning 2019 to 2024, the authors compare XGBoost and elastic-net GLM pricing models for mortality, morbidity, and lapse risk, then use SHAP values and an instrumental-variable approach based on night-shift timing to isolate which features drive unfair pricing outcomes, measured through statistical parity difference, disparate impact ratio, and equalized odds gap. The result that matters most is quantifying the compliance-to-capital link directly, unfair pricing in the bottom income quintile exceeds fair benchmarks by 5.8 percent for life and 7.2 percent for health products, translating into roughly 22 basis points of extra Solvency II underwriting capital. Applying adversarial debiasing closes 65 to 82 percent of that pricing gap while adding only about 14 basis points to capital, an estimated 4.8 million euros for a mid-sized insurer. A limitation the authors flag is that the study covers only four large carriers, so results may not generalize to smaller insurers, non-life products, or firms using internal capital models rather than the Solvency II standard formula.

papers.note: Criticises one-shot assessments and absent corrective action, which is a fair description of what most audits currently deliver.
papers.title: A systematic review of algorithm auditing processes to assess bias and risks in AI systems
papers.journal: Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development
papers.explain_beginner: The paper reviews recent research on how people check AI systems for bias and risk. It looked at 22 studies from technology, law, and social sciences. Audits often test models, inspect them, challenge them, or involve affected people, in areas such as medical forecasts, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The review finds current audits are usually too technical, ignore real-life experiences, do not explain whose values matter, happen only once, rarely include affected communities, and seldom lead to fixes. It suggests audits should become ongoing, inclusive, and connected to decisions. This matters because AI increasingly affects important life opportunities.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this review warns that checking AI for bias and risk is often treated as a one-time technical exercise. The paper examined 22 studies across technology, law, and social sciences and found that audits frequently miss real-world context, do not make value trade-offs clear, exclude affected communities, and rarely lead to corrective action. In practice, leaders should not treat an audit report as proof that a system is fair or low-risk. They should fund ongoing, inclusive reviews tied to clear accountability and follow-up fixes. This informs decisions about AI governance, deployment in high-impact areas such as lending, hiring, and medical forecasting, and investment in continuous auditing capabilities.
papers.explain_practitioner: The author performed a structured review of published research on methods for auditing bias and risk in opaque AI. The search covered technology, law, and social science sources and selected 22 recent applied studies. The reviewed work includes numeric comparisons, model checks, stress tests, and stakeholder involvement, with examples in medical forecasting, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The analysis reports recurring weaknesses: overly technical framing, unclear value choices, single-time assessments, little involvement from affected groups, and few corrective actions after audits. Promising directions include subsidiarity analysis, people-focused tools, and corrective coding. The main result is that auditing should become ongoing, whole-system, inclusive, and tied to governance actions.

papers.note: Shows a hiring model looking fair on standard measures while carrying a ten point disparity when measured properly, a direct warning about method choice.
papers.title: The Illusion of Fairness: Auditing Fairness Interventions in Algorithmic Hiring with Audit Studies

reading.body:
Across nine papers, bias in large language models is consistently detected whenever tested, with the strongest prevalence evidence in medical models where 22 of 24 studies found bias, and no single metric or mitigation covers all forms.

The research splits into competing taxonomies. One survey organizes evaluation by data, model, output, and human review; another separates intrinsic bias from extrinsic bias; a third distinguishes medium-sized models addressed through fine-tuning from large models addressed through prompting. These frameworks do not agree on which metric to trust, and several papers state that intrinsic and extrinsic measures are not reliably correlated. A model can pass one fairness test and still produce biased text in generation.

The practical consequence is that bias mitigation is stage-specific, not a single fix. Pre-training data audits, in-training adjustments, and post-hoc output filtering address different failure modes, and a vendor claim about one stage says nothing about the others. The insurance study quantifies this: unfair pricing in the bottom income quintile exceeds fair benchmarks by 5.8 percent for life and 7.2 percent for health products, and adversarial debiasing closes most of that gap while adding only about 14 basis points to capital requirements.

What the data does not show is real-world harm or a certified fix. Most evidence comes from benchmarks and test-bed evaluations, not deployed patient or customer outcomes. The medical review itself flags publication bias, and the cultural commonsense study notes its evaluation datasets are English-only in construction even when translated. None of these papers connects bias to compute, buildings, or power; the binding constraint here is measurement and mitigation design, not infrastructure.
